newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar slides below 123 yen, lowest in a month.
newsitem.headline: Dollar slides below 123 yen, lowest in a month.

text.p: The dollar slid below 123 yen in morning trade on Friday, the first time it had dropped below that level since April 4, traders said.
Japanese government cash bonds and futures also fell, as speculation heightened that the Bank of Japan might tighten its hyper-easy credit stance as early as July.
The greenback has declined for the past four days, in part on worries that central banks may be gearing up to sell the U.S. currency to halt its two-year-long rally.
The dollar had suffered a sharp blow on Thursday, when the Japanese Finance Ministry's Eisuke Sakakibara, known as "Mr Yen" for his ability to sway markets, said it could drop to 103 yen.

On Friday, the dollar first weakened when Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said he hoped a currency agreement by the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations in late April would be "further digested" by the markets.
The dollar then rose again briefly on comments by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, which traders took to imply that further rises in U.S. interest rates were possible.

Financial leaders from the G7 -- Japan, the United States, Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Canada -- said after they met in Washington last month that they would monitor exchange rates and cooperate as appropriate, adding that currency values should reflect fundamentals and excess volatility was undesirable.

The market is sensitive to Japanese official comments and worries over possible dollar-selling intervention because recently strong Tokyo share prices, weak bond prices and Japan's growing current account surplus suggest such intervention could succeed, traders have said.
But some analysts still wonder how willing Japanese authorities are to back their talk with action and question just how committed to a stronger yen officials are.
"There is a fundamental uncertainty about where they believe their interests lie," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.
The weak yen has helped keep Japan's economic recovery on track by boosting exports -- but those rising exports and a growing current account surplus risk fanning trade friction with Washington.
Mitsuzuka said on Friday that he thought Japan's surplus would not again become an international issue because the recovery was being led by domestic demand, not exports.

Speculation that Japan's central bank is mulling a rise in interest rates because of increased confidence in the economic recovery bolstered bearish sentiment towards the dollar and undermined Japanese government bonds and futures.

Government economic planners said in a monthly report on Friday that the economy was recovering gradually and that the negative impact of a sales tax rise to five percent from three percent on April 1 was "within expectations".

Some economists said they did not expect a quick credit tightening, given continued uncertainty about the impact of fiscal tightening on domestic growth and persistent worries about the bad-loan burden at some Japanese banks.
"There is no inflationary reason for them to raise rates, they are still concerned about banks, and there is not enough information about the economy," one foreign economist said.
